scenes.text: Here's the bacterium from the end of the last video, enlarged. It has no nucleus, no mitochondria, no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi body. Yet it releases energy, builds proteins, swims, and copies its DNA, and in ideal conditions some bacteria divide about every twenty minutes. So how does a bacterium carry out every life process without membrane-bound organelles?
There are nine parts to know, so let's tour the cell like a map: start outside and work in through the layers, look at what's inside, then come back out to the parts that stick out.

On the very outside, many bacteria have a capsule: a slimy layer, mostly made of sugars, wrapped around the cell wall. That slime helps the cell in three ways. It stops the cell drying out, it helps it stick to surfaces, like the film that builds up on teeth, and it can help it hide from immune cells. Not every bacterium has a capsule.

Under the capsule is the cell wall. In bacteria it's made of peptidoglycan, a tough mesh of sugar chains joined by short chains of amino acids. You met a wall in plant cells, and here it does the same job with a different material. It gives the cell its shape, and it stops the cell bursting when water moves in. If the wall is damaged, water keeps entering until the cell splits open.

Just inside the wall is the cell membrane, a thin double layer of fat-like molecules called phospholipids. It's partially permeable, which means it lets some substances through and blocks others, so it controls what enters and leaves. And here's the first part of our answer. With no mitochondria, a bacterium uses its cell membrane instead: many of the enzymes that release energy in respiration sit right in the membrane.

Inside the membrane is the cytoplasm, a jelly-like fluid that's mostly water, with nutrients, salts and enzymes dissolved in it. Most of the cell's chemical reactions happen here, and everything else inside floats in it. Because this bacterium is so tiny, substances spread through the whole cell quickly, so it can run without separate compartments.

Now the DNA. With no nucleus, where are the genes? They're on one long, circular chromosome, folded up in a region called the nucleoid. It's a region, not a compartment: there's no membrane around it. The nucleoid holds the genes the cell needs to stay alive and to make new cells.

Many bacteria also carry plasmids: small, separate rings of extra DNA. A plasmid isn't a mini copy of the main chromosome. It carries a few extra genes, such as one that lets the bacterium survive an antibiotic. A bacterium can usually live without its plasmids, but they're copied on their own, and they can be passed to other bacteria. So, the chromosome holds the essentials, and plasmids hold extras that can be shared.

Scattered through the cytoplasm are thousands of ribosomes, the tiny structures where proteins are made, smaller than the ones in your cells. Here's the second part of our answer. Ribosomes aren't wrapped in a membrane in any cell, not even in yours. So a bacterium's ribosomes simply float in the cytoplasm and build proteins right there, with no membrane-bound organelle needed.

Now back out, to the parts that stick out. A flagellum is a long, whip-like tail anchored in the cell membrane. It doesn't lash like a whip, though. A tiny motor at its base spins it, like a propeller, pushing the bacterium through liquid, towards food or away from harm. That's the third part of our answer: moving needs a motor in the membrane, not an organelle.

The short, hair-like threads on the surface are pili. One is a pilus. Pili let a bacterium grip surfaces and other cells, so it isn't washed away. Some pili do something more surprising. A bacterium can use a pilus to connect to a neighbour and pass it a copy of a plasmid. If that plasmid carries an antibiotic resistance gene, the neighbour becomes resistant too, without any new cells being made.

Without membrane-bound organelles, this bacterium gives each job to a simple structure. The membrane controls what crosses it and carries out much of respiration. Ribosomes in the cytoplasm make proteins. The nucleoid holds the essential genes, and plasmids carry extras. Flagella move the cell, and pili hold on. To remember the nine, tour the map: three layers in, four things inside, two things out.

Two exam questions. First. A bacterium lives attached to rocks in a fast-flowing mountain stream, where the rocks sometimes dry out in summer. Identify two structures that would help it survive there, and describe the function of each. Pause here to answer.

Pili are a strong answer: they grip the rock, so the current can't wash the cell away. A capsule works too: its slime helps the cell stick, and it stops the cell drying out when the rocks are exposed. Each time, name the structure, then link its job to the habitat. The classic mistake is saying flagella hold the cell in place.

Second. Bacterium A carries a plasmid with a gene for resistance to an antibiotic. Bacterium B, of the same species, has no plasmid. After the two are grown together, some B cells survive the antibiotic. Describe a plasmid and a pilus, and explain how plasmid transfer could account for this result. Pause here to answer.

A plasmid is a small ring of DNA, separate from the main chromosome, carrying extra genes. A pilus is a short, hair-like projection that attaches to other cells and can transfer DNA. An A cell could have used a pilus to pass a copy of its resistance plasmid to a B cell, so the gene would spread between existing cells. The classic mistake is calling the plasmid a small copy of the main chromosome.

So for any prokaryote question, name the structure, say what it's like, then say what it lets the cell do. Next, we go to the bench: preparing a real specimen, and finding cells under a light microscope.
